strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP safety problem through a substantial comparison: 13 attacks, four attack families, six open- and closed-source LLMs, and 16 policy categories. Direct attacks, transferability, runtime, and prompt length provide complementary perspectives.

The automated judge explicitly addresses misleading refusal phrases, paraphrases, and off-target responses. Validation against 640 responses annotated by three people, with Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87 and 94.84% agreement, provides meaningful evidence of annotation consistency.

The detailed results reveal useful differences between models and attacks, including the competitiveness of simple human-written prompts and the model dependence of obfuscation attacks. Baselines, three repeated runs, hardware details, and acknowledged runtime limitations strengthen the empirical reporting.
weaknesses: The success criterion needs stronger construct validation. Section 5.3 describes label C as answer correctness, whereas Figure 9 tests direct or indirect relevance; label B also accepts willingness. The rule combining A/B/C into success is unspecified. These criteria do not clearly establish useful harmful assistance. Moreover, mapping broad usage-policy categories does not establish that every selected request requires refusal under each provider’s policy, particularly for conditional deployment restrictions. Human agreement supports consistency but does not resolve these validity questions.

The comparison does not adequately control attack budgets. Generation Exploitation receives an any-success-over-50-responses evaluation, while the general metric is described as top-1. The nominal 50 modification steps also entail different numbers of target and auxiliary-model calls across methods. A matched-budget sampling baseline is needed to distinguish benefits from decoding changes from additional attempts. Final prompt length and coarse wall time do not establish the claimed overall performance–efficiency ranking.

Important reproducibility details are missing or inconsistent. Sections 5.4 and 7.1 specify 500 GCG steps, but Table 8 specifies 50, directly affecting both effectiveness and runtime interpretation. The 50 decoding configurations and judge demonstrations are omitted; the manuscript supplies no release link for the exact 160 questions or evaluation implementation. Model snapshots, evaluation dates, and system prompts also need specification. These gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

Baseline fidelity is uncertain for Masterkey. Section 3.3 substitutes rewriting the AIM template because source code is unavailable, without sufficient detail or validation to establish equivalence to the cited method. Results should be identified as an approximation or obtained from a faithful implementation.

Several conclusions exceed the reported evidence. Optimization-based methods do not consistently perform best: AIM achieves the highest ASR on four of six models in Table 2, while parameter-based attacks are evaluated only on three open models. Calling Llama2 unaffected by transfer attacks also overlooks AutoDAN’s 0.39 ASR versus its 0.31 baseline. Categories described as easy to jailbreak can already have higher baseline compliance than average attack success, such as AI Usage Disclosure in Table 3 (0.93 versus 0.68). Report circumvention of baseline refusals separately from raw compliance.

Generality and uncertainty are insufficiently established for the comprehensive claims. Ten questions per category and transfer from only Vicuna provide limited coverage. Repeating experiments three times measures variability on the selected questions, but does not establish robustness to question selection. Clarify what each reported standard deviation summarizes and provide uncertainty for the principal comparisons.
